review_details.text: None in yen. For a USD-based investor it is a currency position: the yen often strengthens in global sell-offs, so it can act as a crash hedge, but it lost value for years while US rates were far above Japan's.

funds.other_risk_detail: This is where the yen turmoil bites. The yen hit about 163 per dollar in late July, prompting a joint US–Japan intervention (Japan reportedly spent around $85bn) that pushed it to 155, but by mid-August most of that gain had reversed. Japan had already spent ¥11.7 trillion in April–May. It traded near 158 on 27 Oct. Pressures: the BoJ held at 1.25% on 30 Oct (8–1 vote) while US rates are near 4%, though it raised its inflation forecast and signalled more hikes; PM Takaichi said on 19 Oct she may issue deficit bonds to fund about ¥10 trillion of tax cuts, with debt at 204% of GDP; and Japan imports almost all its energy. The risk runs both ways: intervention near 160, or a carry-trade unwind in a crash, could lift the yen 5% in days. For a USD-based investor this fund is a currency bet, not cash.

review_details.text: Low-medium. Commodities are driven this year by the Iran war and oil, not AI. A recession would cut demand for oil and metals, and a ceasefire would remove the war premium. Counterparty risk to Goldman Sachs adds a small extra risk.

funds.other_risk_detail: Energy is the largest part of the commodity index, and Brent is about $115, up 75% in a year, because the Strait of Hormuz has been largely closed since March. Iran says it stays shut until the US accepts its conditions, while Saudi, Turkish, Pakistani and Qatari mediators were in Tehran this week. During the brief June truce, Brent fell to about $72; a deal would hit this fund hard. A recession would also cut metals demand. Exposure comes through a Goldman Sachs swap, which adds counterparty risk. On 27 Oct Iran said it was flexible on reopening the strait if the US lifts its blockade within seven days, and Brent fell 1.7%, then rose back to $115.32 on 28 Oct after the US told non-emergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia. Iran now says Hormuz could reopen within 4–5 days if the US lifts its blockade, but talks are reportedly on hold until after the 3 Nov midterms. On 30 Oct a tanker was hit by limpet mines in the strait, the first successful such strike of the war, and Brent rose 2.4%. Over the 31 Oct weekend a draft US–Iran framework was reported, with Hormuz shipping resuming within 7 days of an initial deal, and Iran's negotiators went to Doha. Nothing is agreed yet, and the US has reportedly told Gulf allies to prepare for a short, intense conflict after the 3 Nov election. On 2 Nov Brent fell 7.6% to $104.77 after Iran offered to reopen Hormuz within two days and Trump said Iran wants a deal.

review_details.text: A climate-tilted version of MSCI World (MSCI World Climate Series A). Technology 31.5%, financials 19.5%, health care 11.5%; USD 72%. Master-fund top holdings (30 Sep): NVIDIA 6.8%, Apple 5.0%, Microsoft 4.6%, Amazon 2.8%, Alphabet 2.3%, Tesla 2.1%, Meta 2.0%, AMD 1.9%.

review_details.label: Returns
review_details.text: The feeder's own figures are not public. The master fund's F USD class shows 1 yr +13.4% and about +6.4% p.a. over 5 yrs. YTD is likely close to MSCI World, about +11%.

review_details.label: AI-crash exposure
review_details.text: High, slightly above MSCI World because the climate tilt underweights energy and overweights Tesla and tech.

funds.other_risk_detail: The climate tilt underweights oil and gas just as Brent sits near $115, so the fund lags when energy leads. Policy shifts away from climate targets can hit renewable and EV holdings (Tesla 2.1%). Rate and valuation risks are the same as for fund 4.

funds.fund: Pimco GIS Gbl Investment Grade Credit INST Acc USD
funds.holdings: Actively managed investment-grade corporate bonds from many countries (banks, utilities, industrials and tech issuers), hedged to USD; ~$7bn fund. Can include AI-related company debt such as big-tech and data-centre bonds.
funds.other_risk: AI borrowing is ~10% of big IG bond indices; Oracle CDS ~308 bp; spreads widened at end-Sep

review_details.label: Holds
review_details.text: An actively managed portfolio of investment-grade corporate bonds from at least three countries, hedged to USD; fund size about $7bn.

review_details.label: AI-crash exposure
review_details.text: Low-medium. Big tech and AI infrastructure firms have issued heavy debt to fund data centres. In a crash credit spreads widen, offsetting part of the gain from falling Treasury yields.

funds.other_risk_detail: AI is not only an equity risk. AI-related debt issuance has passed roughly $466–500bn this year and makes up about 10% of the largest long-term IG bond ETFs. Oracle's 5-year CDS more than doubled this year to about 308 bp, and Meta's and NVIDIA's hit records in October. Pimco as a firm bought $18bn of Meta's $27.3bn Hyperion data-centre bond; public data does not show whether this fund holds it. Credit spreads widened into end-September, and high oil and rate hikes add pressure.

review_details.label: Holds
review_details.text: About 490 EM stocks picked by a quant model (value, quality, momentum). Largest: TSMC ~10%, Samsung ~6%, SK Hynix ~4%, Tencent ~2.6%, then Delta Electronics, Alibaba, China Construction Bank, Petrobras, Vale. Roughly China 27%, Taiwan 21%, Korea 17%, India 11–13%.

review_details.label: Returns
review_details.text: YTD +29.0%, 1 yr +42.0%, 3 yr +27.3% p.a., 5 yr +13.4% p.a. (31 Aug), well ahead of its index.

review_details.label: AI-crash exposure
review_details.text: High. Taiwan and Korea chipmakers are about 20% of the fund. A cheap valuation (P/E ~14 vs ~18 for the index) and exposure to banks, energy and materials give some cushion. The 3 months to Aug returned −3.3% as the Korea crash hit.

funds.review_foot: Daily dealing · EM stocks are less liquid in stress
funds.other_risk_detail: Taiwan is about 21% of the fund. China held live-fire drills across five sea areas on 12–17 Oct, coast-guard ships harassed Taiwanese vessels on 18 Oct, and Beijing drafted export curbs on about 40 technologies, including AI and chips, on 16 Oct. On 15 Oct the Taiwan dollar and won slumped as foreigners sold heavily: NT$165bn of Taiwan stocks in one day, and Korean outflows above $10bn for October. The Philippine peso passed 63 per dollar, and India and Indonesia intervened. On 30 Oct the KOSPI fell 3.5% (trading curbs triggered) and SK hynix 7.1% as the US tech sell-off spread. Korea and India import most of their oil, so $115 oil hurts.

funds.fund: Schroder ISF Asian Local Currency Bond C Acc NAV USD
funds.holdings: Government and quasi-government bonds of Asian countries in their own currencies (Indonesia, India, Korea, Singapore, Thailand, China and others), with active currency positions. Returns depend heavily on Asian currencies.
funds.other_risk: Asian currencies under pressure: peso past 63; RBI and BI intervening; oil-importer stress

review_details.label: Holds
review_details.text: Asian government and quasi-government bonds in local currencies (Indonesia, India, Korea, Singapore, Thailand, China and others), with active currency positions.

review_details.label: Returns
review_details.text: YTD +0.3%, 1 yr −0.9%, 3 yr +1.0% p.a., 5 yr +0.6% p.a. (31 Aug). The weakest long-term performer among the bond funds.

review_details.label: AI-crash exposure
review_details.text: Low-medium. Asian currencies, especially the won and Taiwan dollar, tend to weaken when chip stocks fall and money flees to the dollar, which would hurt this fund in USD terms.

funds.other_risk_detail: Much of the USD return comes from currencies. On 15 Oct the Philippine peso passed 63 per dollar for the first time, Indonesia's central bank intervened for the rupiah, and India's sold dollars to support the rupee. Most Asian economies import oil, and US yields above 5% pull capital out of the region. On the positive side, local yields are high, and Asian central banks have room to cut if oil falls.

review_details.label: Returns
review_details.text: The USD C class does not publish trailing returns on public sites. Converting the EUR B class (YTD +27.2%, 1 yr +46.3%) gives roughly YTD +24%, 1 yr +42%, 5 yr about +7% p.a. in USD. In GBP terms it returned +42.9% over 1 yr and +8.3% p.a. over 5 yrs to 31 Jul.

review_details.label: AI-crash exposure
review_details.text: Very high. About 30% sits in TSMC, Samsung, SK hynix and MediaTek, the stocks that drove Korea's 40% crash in July. Memory-chip makers are the most cyclical part of the AI chain.

funds.review_foot: Daily dealing · ongoing charge 1.05% · EM stocks can gap on bad days
funds.other_risk_detail: About 30% sits in TSMC, Samsung, SK hynix and MediaTek, so the Taiwan drills, China's draft tech export controls and the mid-October foreign selling in Taiwan and Korea hit this fund directly. It holds about 50 stocks against Robeco's ~490, so single-stock shocks matter more.

review_details.label: Returns

review_details.label: AI-crash exposure
review_details.text: Low; a moderate hedge. Less rate-sensitive than pure Treasuries, and about a quarter is corporate credit that would lag.

funds.other_risk_detail: Hedged to USD, so no currency risk. The main risk is yields rising further: Pimco's CIO says the 10-year could reach 6% if oil-driven inflation, fiscal worries and leveraged unwinds intensify. A 4.8% starting yield covers roughly a 0.8-point rise in rates over a year before the fund loses money.

review_details.label: Holds
review_details.text: MSCI Japan, 168 stocks. Top 10 (30 Sep): MUFG 4.7%, Toyota 3.3%, Tokyo Electron 3.1%, SMFG 3.0%, Advantest 3.0%, Hitachi 2.9%, SoftBank Group 2.8%, Recruit 2.6%, Sony 2.6%, Kioxia 2.5%. P/E 17.2.

review_details.label: Returns
review_details.text: Vanguard's site did not show trailing returns. From published NAVs I estimate about +14% YTD to 30 Sep and about +10% to 26 Oct in yen, after a roughly 4% October drop.

review_details.label: AI-crash exposure
review_details.text: Medium. Tokyo Electron, Advantest, SoftBank and Kioxia (~11%) are direct AI plays; banks and autos are not. For a USD-based investor, the yen typically strengthens in a global sell-off, which cushions losses.

funds.other_risk_detail: Priced in yen, so for a USD-based investor the yen's slide (from about 151 when Takaichi took office a year ago to 157–163) has cut returns. Japanese stocks fell for three straight weeks to 26 Oct (Nikkei 62,189), led by Tokyo Electron and Advantest. Further BoJ hikes would lift the yen, which helps USD-based holders but hurts exporters; deficit-funded tax cuts and JGB yields near 3% unsettle both bonds and the currency. Japan imports almost all its energy.

review_details.label: Holds
review_details.text: 340 US Treasury and agency bonds (98.8% Treasuries), rated AA+. Yield to worst 5.12%, average duration 5.4 years, 58% maturing in 1–5 years.

review_details.label: AI-crash exposure
review_details.text: Low; the clearest hedge of the 28 funds if a crash pushes the Fed to cut. A 1-point fall in yields would add roughly 5% on top of the 5% yield. It does not hedge an inflation shock.

funds.review_foot: Daily dealing · ongoing charge 0.12% · Treasuries are the most liquid bonds in the world
funds.other_risk_detail: This fund hedges a growth crash but not an inflation shock. September CPI was 3.7%. The Fed held on 28 Oct, but two dissenters wanted a hike and Fitch expects one to 4.25% in December (markets priced about 78% odds on 29 Oct). The 10-year yield rose to 5.04% on 28 Oct, then fell back to 4.98% on 29 Oct as Big Tech sold off, and the 27 Oct 5-year auction was the 12th weak one in a row. Heavy Treasury issuance, and Japanese investors bringing money home as JGB yields rise, could also push yields up. A 5.1% starting yield is a strong cushion.
